How Dragon Con Became an Unexpected Place for Couples to Meet and Get Married

September 16, 2026 by John Struck
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 6:39
Instaread

Cosplay, celebrity panels, gaming sessions, elaborate costumes, late-night parties, and packed hotel lobbies usually come to mind when people picture Dragon Con.

Romance probably sits much lower on that list.

Dragon Con began in 1987 with roughly 1,200 attendees. By 2022, attendance had climbed past 85,000 members, helping turn the Atlanta event into the world’s largest fan-run, multi-genre pop-culture convention.

Behind those numbers sits another story. Thousands of people spend several days surrounded by others who understand their favorite characters, obscure franchises, hobbies, inside jokes, and creative interests.

Some attendees meet friends. Others meet partners. A few later, they return wearing costumes for an occasion much bigger than another convention weekend.

Could a convention built around fandom also be one of the most natural places for two like-minded people to fall in love?

Why Dragon Con Brings People Together

Dragon Con puts tens of thousands of people into an environment where starting a conversation requires very little effort.

Spot someone dressed as a character you love, recognize a reference on a T-shirt, or sit beside another fan at a panel and an opening already exists.

Programming adds even more chances to find people with matching interests.

Dragon Con offered 32 programming tracks in 2022, covering subjects such as Star Wars, high fantasy, writing, costuming, puppetry, and space.

Physical layout also changes how people interact. Events take place across five downtown Atlanta hotels and AmericasMart rather than inside one isolated convention hall.

Attendees constantly cross paths while moving among panels, restaurants, elevators, hotel atriums, parties, and costume gatherings.

Social life barely slows after scheduled programming ends. Several parts of Dragon Con contribute to that atmosphere:

  • Hotel atriums regularly become informal meeting areas filled with conversations, costumes, dancing, and photography.
  • Parties take place inside hotel rooms, lobbies, and ballrooms throughout the convention.
  • Cosplay gives strangers an immediate reason to approach one another without needing an awkward introduction.
  • Multi-day attendance creates repeated encounters instead of limiting an interaction to one short event.

Regular attendees sometimes describe Dragon Con as a 24/7 convention. Nightlife has even earned comparisons to a “Nerd Mardi Gras,” which captures how little separation exists between formal programming and spontaneous socializing.

From Shared Fandom to Relationships

Shared interests can remove much of the uncertainty that comes with meeting someone new. Conversation already has somewhere to go when both people care about the same game, series, author, costume technique, or fictional universe.

Similar compatibility cues matter in online dating too, where platforms such as https://ladadate.com/ukrainian-brides let people consider interests and relationship goals before deciding to start a conversation.

Dragon Con’s enormous programming schedule makes extremely specific connections possible.

One attendee recalled entering a panel devoted to a very niche subject and discovering about 20 other people who cared about exactly the same thing. That same person also described meeting someone by chance at Dragon Con and planning to keep in contact after the convention ended.

Small interactions can matter because Dragon Con is not necessarily a one-time event for its attendees. Many people return every year, sometimes with the same friends, cosplay groups, or online communities.

Annual attendance gives relationships a different rhythm. Someone met casually one year might become a familiar face the next. Online conversations can continue between conventions.

Romantic relationships can grow through that same cycle. Dragon Con then becomes attached not only to a favorite fandom but also to memories involving a partner.

For some couples, returning to Atlanta eventually raises an obvious question.

If Dragon Con played such a large role in bringing two people together, why celebrate their marriage somewhere else?

Why Couples Get Married at Dragon Con

Ballrooms, matching decorations, formal dress codes, and standard reception traditions can feel disconnected to people whose relationship developed through cosplay, gaming, fantasy, or science fiction.

Dragon Con gives those couples another option, even though the convention itself does not officially conduct or organize weddings.

Attendees largely arrange ceremonies independently, creating celebrations around their own interests.

Ashley Paramore and Justin Robert Young celebrated their marriage at Dragon Con in 2015. Returning carried special meaning because they had originally met at the convention.

Game of Thrones and Battlestar Galactica influenced their wedding costumes, tying their ceremony directly to the culture that had helped bring them together.

Emily and Chase Swiatek took a similar route in 2017 after deciding that conventional wedding plans were becoming too expensive and did not feel like them. Costumes turned their ceremony into something far more personal:

  • Chase dressed as Link, the hero of *The Legend of Zelda*.
  • Emily dressed as Navi, Link’s fairy companion.
  • Their officiant appeared as Deadpool.

Emily later described the experience as combining a themed wedding they actually wanted with a “mini honeymoon.”

Dragon Con as a Community

Weddings reveal something about Dragon Con that attendance figures cannot fully capture. People are not simply gathering to consume entertainment. Many build lasting social circles there.

Kevin and Laura Close had already legally married in New York when they held another celebration during Dragon Con in 2017.

Motivation centered on people rather than paperwork. Friends they regularly saw in Georgia mattered enough that the couple wanted another celebration that included them.

Their event took place outside SunTrust Plaza. Kevin wore a Wyndham Hotels Wizard costume, while Laura dressed as Sophie in *Howl’s Moving Castle*.

Choosing Dragon Con made sense because their convention friends had become part of their social life.

A yearly fan event had effectively created a recurring meeting point for a group that might otherwise be scattered across different cities or states.

Fan-run culture helps support that connection. Many attendees describe community-building as one of Dragon Con’s defining traits.

Celebrity appearances and vendors matter, but conversations in hotel lobbies, friendships formed in programming tracks, shared meals, group costumes, and yearly reunions give the convention much of its social character.

Dragon Con Media Relations Director Dan Carroll captured that idea neatly when discussing convention weddings. Dragon Con might begin as a celebration of things people love, yet sometimes attention shifts toward the people they love.

Summary

Nobody needed to design Dragon Con as a matchmaking event for relationships to happen there.

Bringing tens of thousands of people together around shared interests already creates favorable conditions for conversation, friendship, and repeated contact.

Annual attendance adds another ingredient. People do not necessarily disappear after one weekend. They reconnect online, return the following year, introduce friends, join groups, and gradually build a social network tied to Atlanta.

Fan-run culture strengthens that pattern by giving attendees countless informal spaces to interact outside scheduled panels.

Relationships can start beside a cosplay photo area, inside a hotel lobby, at a party, during a niche discussion, or through friends met during earlier conventions.

John Struck
